An Investigation Into The Impacts Of COVID-19 on New York City Taxi Data

Introduction

Cities have been a discussion topic for network analysts for the past century, how they interact with each other, why certain cities are connected, and why certain links form between certain groups. Urban cities are a point of interest for network analysts due to their ever-growing nature which increases the different networks within a city ​(Batty, 2013)​. A network refers to the interaction between nodes and edges, an example of this is different city destinations (nodes) and the edges would be the number of transports between them. Networks can be influenced by a wide range of variables, for example, Fang et al 2020 presents how spatial link intensity is important when discussing how agglomeration can impact the business hubs within a city and how this interacts with other hubs ​(Fang et al., 2020)​. Networks can also be altered by different variables such as weather, time of year and even the time of day.

This report will investigate the Network Analysis of the New York Taxi System, focusing on the Yellow Taxi. Founded in 1912 The New York Taxi System is a fundamental part of New York and is how many commuters get around the city ​(Ulak, Yazici and Aljarrah, 2020)​. The New York Taxi System can reflect the environment around it, for example, if there are fewer trips during the day this could suggest that it is a weekday or a less busy day. The New York Taxi System data is increasingly important with the rise in people conforming to the use of Uber as it is viewed as more ‘convenient’ ​(Willis and Tranos, 2021)​, this data can reflect the impact Uber and Lyft are having and how the network is changing.

This report will focus on the differences in the New York Yellow Taxi Data set before, during and post-COVID-19. By visualising the differences in the taxi data at each of those times it can present whether there are certain differences in the New York Taxi Data, whether any new hubs and clustering have emerged from this and how significant this is. This report will include the aims of this project as well as a literature review explaining different theories, the methods used, the results found and a discussion of the data as to why this is significant.

 

Aims And Objectives:

  • To understand the influence COVID-19 has had on the New York Yellow Taxi System

  • To construct spatial networks of the NewYork Yellow Taxi system, with the nodes being the different drop-off and pick-up points.

  • To Discuss why the New York Yellow Taxi System is so significant.

Literature Review

Spatial Network Analysis

Spatial Networks are becoming increasingly important when studying network analysis and when looking into urban studies. There has been an increasing interest in this since the publication of Sassen’s ‘The Global city` ​(Pflieger and Rozenblat, 2010)​ which presents the idea of how significant flows are between and within cities are and how there can be issues because of this. Pflieger and Rozenblat in particular present the disparity between urban networks and social networks, unlike the traditional social network where it is believed that everything is interconnected, Pflieger and Rozenblat argue that urban networks are different. Instead, these networks connect only to particular networks which serve a distinct purpose for example business hubs or areas of stores. These networks can be influenced on an individual level as well as on a larger scale for example a corporation moving areas. New spatial hubs can also emerge which can affect a network and can even create a whole new network which can be linked in between. An example of this is if a big company such as Deloitte had multiple offices in London but then opened one in Manchester, the movement of one of these ‘nodes’ expands the network and allows for new clusters to arrive as agglomeration can occur. Agglomeration refers to nodes which are clustered together which are benefiting from being close together for example business hubs ​(Johansson and Quigley, 2004)​. Spatial Networks can be measured by different variables for example the degree of centrality, betweenness, and clustering. These measures will be explained later in the report. Similar studies have been conducted before to understand commuting flows within major cities, for example, Hamedmoghadam-Rafati et al (2017) researched the New York Taxi Trips, this research adopts an approach where they developed a large-scale mobility network which was weighted and directed​(Hamedmoghadam-Rafati et al., 2017)​. It is important to understand that these network systems are significant and being able to understand the location of the clusters allows for planners to use this information to adapt future transport links.

The importance of the New York Taxi System

The New York Taxi System is a fundamental aspect of New York. Not only from a tourist point of view is it an iconic part of New York history, but it also helps many people from day to day to get to where they need to be. For example, in reference to urban mobility on peak days New York Yellow Taxis can accumulate over 450,000 trips a day ​(N. Ferreira et al., 2013)​. This can result in thousands of different locations being connected all over. Although there are arguments about what will happen to New York Taxis, as with an increase in external taxi companies such as Uber and Lyft there has been a pull away from the traditional yellow cabs ​(Willis and Tranos, 2021)​. Furthermore, it is significant to understand the New York Taxi System and its role in urban mobility. The industry itself brings in around 30% of fares paid by all passengers using different forms of taxi systems and even more than 40% in the area of Manhattan ​(Gandhi, Gorod and Sauser, 2011)​. Although there are other forms of transport which are significant to New York such as the subway and bus systems, the yellow cab network represents the significant hubs of New York City. Key hubs of New York include Manhattan and JFK. When going through this investigation it is important to keep the significance of the New York Taxi system in mind and how it helps the mobility of the city even though there are other forms of transport.

The Impact Of Covid-19 On Transport Systems

COVID-19 had a detrimental impact on various networks, even 5 years on, the effects of COVID-19 have a lasting impact on our networks. Transport networks took one of the hardest hits. This was due to a decrease in people travelling due to travel restrictions, in particular, travel to JFK would be limited as people would not be travelling back and forth from the area to fly. To this very moment people are still restricting their use of public transport, this is due to the fear of contamination which was present previously during ultimate COVID-19 infections and has carried on to now ​(Nian et al., 2020)​. Other issues in the transport sector included that when there was transport available it was still limited as many companies had to enforce social distancing. This has impacted the urban mobility and transport systems as this has reduced the number of passengers for public transport ​(Abduljabbar, Liyanage and Dia, 2022)​. However, it could be argued that with a reduction in the use of public transport such as trains and buses, there could be an increase in Taxi trips instead as there are limitations on the number of people you are in contact with ​(Abduljabbar, Liyanage and Dia, 2022)​. Transport systems are significant networks as they are directly interlinked with other networks, and they are the backbone of many cities. An example of this is presented in Arimura, 2020 where their investigation found that in Sapporo Japan, the business district population density was reduced by 90% due to travel restrictions ​(Arimura et al., 2020)​. Furthermore, since Covid-19 emerged the concept of working from home has become more popular, as a result, a significant amount of people only go to the office one day a week, further hindering transport networks. Overall COVID-19 has had detrimental impacts on transport systems including taxis due to the reduction of people who travel.

Methods

The data used within this investigation has been obtained from theTLC Trip Record Data, specifically, this report analyses data from three key years, 2017, 2020 and 2023. 2017 was three years before the peak of COVID-19, 2020 was the peak of COVID-19 and 2023 was the time life had returned to somewhat ‘normal’. The month chosen to analyse New York Yellow Taxi Data was July. July was chosen as this is peak tourism season and would show how complex the network system is. This data was then loaded into R and analysed separately to begin with. The data used is formatted as a paraquet, as a result, the function arrow was required to load the data in.

New York Taxi Data 2017

library(arrow)

taxi_data_2017 <- read_parquet("yellow_tripdata_2017-07 (1).parquet")

From the data presented it is shown that the dates are correct and the data can be used.

To create this network, it is crucial to decide what the nodes and edges are within this project. Within this project it was decided that the nodes would be the Pickup (PULocationID) and Drop off (DOLocationID) locations. Whilst the Edges would be the travel between this. To create the nodes, Pick Up and Drop off locations were combined into one vector and then the distinct locations were pulled out of this.

# This combines the nodes together and then distinguishes the different locations 
nodes_2017 <- unique(c(taxi_data_2017$PULocationID, taxi_data_2017$DOLocationID))
# Identifying the edges within the network by presenting the distance between the drop off locations and pick up locations
edges_2017 <- data.frame(from = paste(taxi_data_2017$PULocationID),
                        to = paste(taxi_data_2017$DOLocationID))

For later use when analysing descriptive statistics such as degree centrality and betweeness, the nodes and edges are made into a singular data frame.

library(igraph)
graph_2017 <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_2017, directed = TRUE) #`directed = TRUE' implies that the edges have direction

To minimise the data further, this investigation reduced the taxi trips to those under 50 miles which would suggest it is only contained to New York City and the surrounding areas.

taxi_data_2017 <- subset(taxi_data_2017, trip_distance < 50 ) # the subset function allows for subsets to be returned for specific variavkes such as the trip distance under 50 miles

To further reduce the data observed in the investigation to obtain a clearer view of the network at hand, this report is primarily using data from the busiest day of July month. The following code represents the method for finding out the busiest day of the month.

taxi_data_2017$tpep_pickup_datetime <- as.POSIXct(taxi_data_2017$tpep_pickup_datetime)

taxi_data_2017$date <- as.Date(taxi_data_2017$tpep_pickup_datetime)

tpd_2017 <- table(taxi_data_2017$date) #tdp_2017 refers to trips per day
# This allows for the data to be grouped by their date
library(dplyr)
tpd_2017 <- taxi_data_2017 %>%
  group_by(date) %>%
  summarise(trip_count = n())

Using the ggplot2 function, this can present a histogram which shows the different days of July and what days have different amounts of trips. The ggplot2 function was used as this function allows for the user to customise the graph to the extent wanted.

Figure 1: Histogram of Taxi Trips per day in July 2017 within New York CIty

As shown in the head above the busiest day of Taxi trips for July 2017 was the 20th. As a result, this investigation for 2017 will be focusing on this date.

# Extracting only the busiest days data from the original 'taxi_data_2017'

busiest_days_2017<- "2017-07-20"  

bdd_2017 <- subset(taxi_data_2017, date == busiest_days_2017)

Once the day has been chosen, the nodes and edges have to be recreated for the new network analysis.

# Extract pickup(PULocationID) and drop off(DOLocationID) points for the busiest day
nodes_bd_2017 <- unique(cbind(bdd_2017$PULocationID,bdd_2017$DOLocationID))

# Create a unique node identifier for each unique location
nodes_bd_2017 <- unique(data.frame(longitude = nodes_bd_2017[, 1], latitude = nodes_bd_2017[, 2]))
# Creating the edges between the busiest day data from pickup and drop off points
edges_bd_2017 <- data.frame(
  from = paste(bdd_2017$PULocationID),
  to = paste(bdd_2017$DOLocationID))

The following code makes sure each of the nodes and edges are unique so when the network graph is created the overlap is limited.

# Ensuring that the pickup and dropoff coordinates are unique
bdd_2017$pickup_id <- paste(bdd_2017$PULocationID)
bdd_2017$dropoff_id <- paste(bdd_2017$DOLocationID)

# Combining pickup and dropoff IDs to create unique nodes
nodes_bd_2017 <- unique(cbind(bdd_2017$pickup_id, bdd_2017$dropoff_id))

# This creates a data frame of unique nodes with unique names
nodes_df_2017 <- data.frame(id = unique(c(bdd_2017$pickup_id, bdd_2017$dropoff_id)))
# Creating an edge list using the unique identifiers
edges_bd_2017 <- data.frame(
  from = bdd_2017$pickup_id,
  to = bdd_2017$dropoff_id
)

Using the new edges and nodes a new network graph can be created which will be presented below.

library(igraph)

# Creating the graph
taxi_graph_2017 <- graph_from_data_frame(edges_bd_2017, directed = TRUE, vertices = nodes_df_2017)

# Plotting the network using base R
plot(taxi_graph_2017, vertex.size = 5, vertex.label = NA, edge.arrow.size = 0.5)

Figure 2: Network Map of New York Taxi Data July 20th 2017 

# Saving the map as a PNG for easier analysis later, can also combine with the other networks.

# Open the PNG device to save the plot
png("nyc_taxi_2017.png", width = 800, height = 600)

# Plotting the map
plot(taxi_graph_2017, vertex.size = 5, vertex.label = NA, edge.arrow.size = 0.5)

# Turn off the device to save the file
dev.off()

  to = paste(bdd_2020$DOLocationID))
# Ensuring that the pickup and dropoff coordinates are unique
bdd_2020$pickup_id <- paste(bdd_2020$PULocationID)
bdd_2020$dropoff_id <- paste(bdd_2020$DOLocationID)

# Combining pickup and dropoff IDs to create unique nodes
nodes_bd_2020 <- unique(cbind(bdd_2020$pickup_id, bdd_2020$dropoff_id))

# This creates a data frame of unique nodes with unique names
nodes_df_2020 <- data.frame(id = unique(c(bdd_2020$pickup_id, bdd_2020$dropoff_id)))
# Creating an edge list using the unique identifiers
edges_bd_2020 <- data.frame(
  from = bdd_2020$pickup_id,
  to = bdd_2020$dropoff_id
)
library(igraph)

# Creating the graph

library(gridExtra)

# Loading the images
img_2017 <- readPNG("nyc_Taxi_2017.png")

img_2023 <- readPNG("nyc_Taxi_2023.png")

# Converting them to raster objects
g_2017 <- rasterGrob(img_2017, interpolate = TRUE)
g_2020 <- rasterGrob(img_2020, interpolate = TRUE)
g_2023 <- rasterGrob(img_2023, interpolate = TRUE)

# Creating labels for each plot
label_2017 <- textGrob("NYC Taxi Network 2017", gp = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"))
label_2020 <- textGrob("NYC Taxi Network 2020", gp = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"))
label_2023 <- textGrob("NYC Taxi Network 2023", gp = gpar(fontsize = 10, fontface = "bold"))

# Combining the image and the label into one grob for each year
g_2017_labeled <- arrangeGrob(g_2017, label_2017, ncol = 1, heights = unit(c(10, 1), "cm"))
g_2020_labeled <- arrangeGrob(g_2020, label_2020, ncol = 1, heights = unit(c(10, 1), "cm"))
g_2023_labeled <- arrangeGrob(g_2023, label_2023, ncol = 1, heights = unit(c(10, 1), "cm"))

# Combining the labeled images into a single layout (1 row, 3 columns)
combined_plot <- grid.arrange(g_2017_labeled, g_2020_labeled, g_2023_labeled, ncol = 3)

Centrality Measures

Furthermore, once we have investigated all the different network graphs, to further analyse the data at present, the degree centrality other measures will be analysed as follows. Using the data previously collected. Using the Kable function we can present the different variables.

Centralities 2017

# Calculating degree centrality
V(graph_2017)$degree <- degree(graph_2017, mode = "all")
V(graph_2017)$in_degree <- degree(graph_2017, mode = "in")
V(graph_2017)$out_degree <- degree(graph_2017, mode = "out")
# Calculating betweenness centrality
V(graph_2017)$betweenness <- betweenness(graph_2017, directed = TRUE, normalized = TRUE)
# Calculating closeness centrality
V(graph_2017)$closeness <- closeness(graph_2017, mode = "all", normalized = TRUE)
# Calculating eigenvector centrality
V(graph_2017)$eigenvector <- eigen_centrality(graph_2017, directed = TRUE)$vector
# Creating a data frame of node-level measures
node_metrics <- data.frame(
  Degree = V(graph_2017)$degree,        # Degree centrality
  InDegree = V(graph_2017)$in_degree,  # In-degree centrality
  OutDegree = V(graph_2017)$out_degree, # Out-degree centrality
  Betweenness = V(graph_2017)$betweenness, # Betweenness centrality
  Closeness = V(graph_2017)$closeness, # Closeness centrality
  Eigenvector = V(graph_2017)$eigenvector   # PageRank scores
)

Results

This result section will comprise the major findings from this investigation, from the network graphs and the centrality measures presented from the previous coding. To easily visualise the differences between the three years being presented in this investigation, the different years have been combined into one singular graph for comparison purposes.

combined_plot <- grid.arrange(g_2017_labeled, g_2020_labeled, g_2023_labeled, ncol = 3)

Figure 8: Taxi Network maps from 2017,2020 and 2023 combined to visualise easier

From table 4,5 and 6 we can see the centrality measures for each of the nodes. The ones of specific importance when understanding this network are the overall degree of centrality and the betweenness centrality. The degree of centrality represents the number of links one node has with other nodes within the network ​(Ergün and Usluel, 2016)​ in this case it would be how interconnected these locations are. The higher the degree of centrality suggests the more significant a network is. In comparison, betweenness centrality represents the nodes which lay on a path which is connecting other nodes. The higher the betweenness centrality means these nodes have more influence than others.

New York Taxi Network 2017

The NYC Taxi Network presents a network which has not been affected by COVID-19. As a result, we have the assumption this is what the normal network of New York Taxi systems presents. This Graph presents a high-density network. A high-density network explains within this network many of the nodes are close together suggesting the taxi system is used for more short-range journeys. Even though this network has a high-density, the network is relatively dispersed as presented by the various nodes reaching out further than the central cluster. There seems to be more of a diverse range of nodes spreading out further towards the west of the city. This suggests more people commute to that area. This could be due to work areas, the suburbs or transport links being near those nodes.

New York Taxi Network 2020

In comparison to the 2017 network analysis data the nodes within this data set for 2020 are more densely compact together and there is less variety in the distance the nodes are away. There are still nodes which are not in the centre of New York, however, the amount is a lot lower than in 2017, and different to the 2017 data we do not see this cluster of nodes to the west of the city which could represent workplaces or more tourist attractions which would not be in use because of COVID-19. However it is important to note this data is taken from July 2020, which was when COVID-19 had calmed down a bit so there was travel, however as presented in the maps above people are travelling more locally and shorter distances.

New York Taxi Network 2023

Lastly, the 2023 New York Taxi Data presents the network connections of New York Yellow Taxi post-COVID-19. At this point, transport networks should have resumed normality as COVID-19 had settled down. However, as mentioned before there are lasting impacts on transport as COVID-19 has changed the way networks work. The 2023 network is similar to the pre-COVID 2017 network with there being a cluster of nodes in the centre and then with more spread out the further from the centre you get. The significant difference between them is there are even more edges between the nodes centrally and more nodes further out creating a circular shape to the network which shows new important areas forming.

Discussion

Through the data gathered from this investigation, it is clear that COVID-19 has affected the network of the New York Taxi System. As shown in figure 7 the network is more condensed and has less diversity compared to the years 2017 and 2023. However, even three years on from Covid-19 the New York Taxi Network is not where it used to be. This means that this network is less connected than it used to be and no longer holds a significant place in the general transport networks of New York. Furthermore, it can be seen through other variables such as the Eigenvector variable. For example, for node 1 the Eigenvector variable for 2017 was 1, whilst for 2023 the value was 0.94. Although this does not seem like a big jump it is a difference that if networks returned to normal after COVID-19, would not have happened. The Eigenvector variable is significant as it shows the influence nodes have on a network. Many may argue that the difference is not that much and what is the significance of a node being highly connected, the more connected a node is on a network the more beneficial it is. In this instance, New York Yellow Taxi drivers may have more interactions, or if their nodes have more connections they may have a higher potential of picking up passengers at the same place they dropped off which helps their business and which further helps the network to keep going. So, what is the issue if this network becomes less connected and slowly the nodes and edges decrease? This network is significant for many people’s day travel and as the network becomes less connected it will be less efficient and both the passengers and cab drivers will benefit less. However, this could mean that a new network could be created or that previously existing networks such as train systems of the subway may have to offer new links in the future such as expansion of routes. This is directly influenced by COVID-19 as COVID-19 reduced the number of people making trips each day and also instilled a fear of transport due to.

Not only does COVID-19 directly influence the network by reducing the number of passengers, but it will have a further effect on those who rely on these passengers for their livelihood such as the taxi drivers. By understanding these network measures and where different clusters are within New York, councils can help to mitigate changes to these networks to help increase incentives to use them. For example, if fewer people are using taxis, those in charge of the transport network can introduce easier ways to get taxis or offer promotions to try to increase those travelling in a certain area. It is important for people in the future to measure transport networks if there is a significant cluster in a certain area of New York City with significant passengers and edges, transport companies can try and increase the number of taxis in that area to further help the network.

Overall, the data shows that the network of New York Taxi data has changed since 2017, and it is predominately because of COVID-19 and the increase of people working from home. This is not to say that this has changed for the worse, instead it is different, and the network changed to support the different needs of the area. The data shows also that even though the network has changed there are still a significant number of nodes and people using Yellow Taxi Cabs, as mentioned before this is because they are a pinnacle part of New York history. However, it is important to remember that this data is only representative of one day in one month. In the future, it is suggested to use a bigger data set of all the months and instead focus on a specific area of New York City. In the future, this data can also be combined with data such as where businesses are located or other commuting networks such are the subway to see if other forms of transport networks have been influenced similarly.

Conlusions

In conclusion, networks are subject to change because the world around us is always changing. COVID-19 has influenced the network structure of New York Taxis by changing where different clusters are gathering. However, network changes are not always a bad thing as this can introduce new variables into a network and can cause the network to expand. But it is increasingly important to preserve the New York Taxi network as it is the backbone of the city and is a fundamental part of the history. This research has shown that the network of New York Yellow Taxis is still relied on heavily and should be preserved.
